text: Could someone place all these pictures on a handmade Neocities page by writing code? Let's look at one choice the maker actually made.
The snail goes beside the note when there is room. This little stamp is another picture, attached to the postcard. Both screens use the same files.
Before we resize: what do you think will happen to the snail and the note on a narrow screen?
Let's narrow it. Now the note stacks below the picture. The same rules keep the stamp attached to the postcard.
A PNG screenshot freezes layout and text. An SVG can stay crisp and may contain selectable text, but scaling a fixed composition is not the same as HTML reflowing.
Start in a plain text editor. Save index dot html. HTML describes the things on the page and their order. A separate style sheet describes how they look and fit together.
The postcard section contains the snail image, a note, and the decorative stamp image. The snail's alternative text describes it for someone who cannot see it.
Open the page locally in a browser. Here we use a small local server. The browser reads the HTML and its linked style sheet, then draws the result.
Without a special layout rule, blocks normally follow one another. The note comes after the picture. That ordinary flow is our starting point.
A drag might say put the snail at one coordinate. Our author can say: put the picture beside the note when there is room, but keep both readable when there isn't.
The postcard is the parent box. Its grid rule places the image and the note. This columns rule fits as many columns as it can, aiming for a minimum of two hundred sixty pixels each.
If the available space becomes too narrow for two columns, predict where the note will go.
The note goes below the image. The browser measures the space and keeps their order, using the same rule.
The stamp has a different rule. The postcard is positioned relative, making it a reference box. The stamp is positioned absolute, outside normal flow, so it can overlap.
Let's move one actual picture. The stamp starts twelve pixels from the postcard's right edge. Change right to one hundred pixels, save, and refresh.
Here are the real browser results at the same width. The stamp moved left by eighty eight pixels. The postcard, snail, and note stayed put.
Narrow the browser, and the stamp stays one hundred pixels from the postcard's right side. It can overlap the picture.
View Source shows the original HTML loaded for the page. Inspector shows the live document tree and computed layout. Find the postcard, its picture and note, and the stamp.
Your turn. Change the stamp's right value to forty pixels. Predict which way it moves, save, refresh, and check. Then narrow the browser. What is the stamp attached to?
To share the page, upload index dot html, style dot css, snail dot svg, garden dot svg, and stamp dot svg to a static host. Neocities also has a browser editor.
A free Neocities address follows the pattern site name dot neocities dot org. The host serves the files, and each visitor's browser lays them out for its own screen.

The maker chose the relationships: snail beside note when it fits, stamp on postcard, pictures in a gallery. The browser does the measuring. That's how typed instructions can make a page feel handmade.
